per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: Primary pulmonary artery sarcoma (angiosarcoma type) of the main pulmonary trunk and right pulmonary artery — NOT pulmonary embolism / chronic thromboembolic pulmonary disease as initially presumed.

HOW CONFIRMED: Intraoperative histopathology. The patient was taken to surgery for embolectomy of a presumed chronic thrombotic mass in the pulmonary trunk; histopathological examination of the resected material revealed angiosarcoma of the pulmonary artery (angiosarcoma accounts for ~7% of pulmonary artery sarcomas). The "filling defect" repeatedly seen on imaging was tumor, not thrombus.

KEY DISCRIMINATORS THAT POINTED AWAY FROM PE: (1) No predisposing/risk factors for venous thromboembolism and no prior VTE; (2) Lower-extremity venous duplex negative for DVT; (3) Failure to respond to anticoagulation — recurrent massive haemoptysis and persistent/progressive imaging despite therapeutic anticoagulation over months; (4) A discrete mass in the pulmonary trunk on transesophageal echocardiography; (5) Pulmonary angiography described occlusion as due to "external compression or intra-luminal infiltration" rather than simple embolic clot; (6) Constitutional symptoms (fever, exhaustion, weight of illness), haemoptysis, and mediastinal lymphadenopathy — features atypical for bland PE and suggestive of malignancy. The unilateral fixed perfusion defect plus an enlarging intraluminal filling defect refractory to anticoagulation is the classic pulmonary artery sarcoma masquerade.

CORRECT DISPOSITION/TREATMENT: Recognize that an intraluminal pulmonary artery filling defect that does not resolve with adequate anticoagulation, in a patient without VTE risk factors and without DVT, should raise suspicion for pulmonary artery sarcoma. Definitive management is surgical resection (pulmonary endarterectomy/tumor resection, potentially with reconstruction) for diagnosis and possible cure/debulking, followed by adjuvant chemotherapy/radiotherapy. Prognosis is poor when diagnosis is delayed. In the source case, diagnosis came only at surgery; the patient was haemodynamically unstable post-operatively, required invasive mechanical ventilation, and died of cardiopulmonary failure ~3 weeks later.

Percutaneous/transluminal biopsy is discouraged due to bleeding risk.

per_case.plain_answer_text:
MOST LIKELY DIAGNOSIS: Primary pulmonary artery sarcoma (PAS) — most often an intimal sarcoma of the pulmonary trunk/right pulmonary artery. A leiomyosarcoma or undifferentiated intimal sarcoma is the leading histologic subtype; the chief alternative malignant mimic is an angiosarcoma.

RECOMMENDED NEXT ACTION: Stop treating this as bland thromboembolism and pursue a tissue/operative diagnosis of an intraluminal pulmonary artery tumor. Concretely: (1) obtain a PET-CT (an FDG-avid, hypermetabolic filling defect strongly favors tumor over thrombus and helps stage), and (2) proceed to definitive sampling/intervention — referral to a center for pulmonary endarterectomy-style surgical resection (which provides both diagnosis and the only potentially curative therapy) or, if not an immediate surgical candidate, image-guided/endovascular or transvenous biopsy of the mass. Discontinue reliance on anticoagulation alone and manage in a multidisciplinary thoracic oncology/cardiothoracic setting; consider neoadjuvant or adjuvant chemo/radiation per sarcoma protocol after histology.

CONFIDENCE: Moderate-to-high (roughly 75–80%) for "a primary intraluminal malignancy of the pulmonary artery (intimal/leiomyosarcoma) rather than thromboembolic disease." Lower confidence on the exact histologic subtype until biopsy.

BRIEF REASONING:
- The clinical course is the key discriminator. A pulmonary arterial filling defect that does not resolve or stabilize after roughly six months of adequate anticoagulation, and in fact progresses, argues strongly against bland thromboembolus.
- No VTE risk factors, no DVT on bilateral duplex, and a completely normal hypercoagulability/coagulation panel (normal platelets, fibrinogen, PT/aPTT/TT, protein C and protein S) make embolic clot from a peripheral source very unlikely — a clot occluding the entire right PA with no detectable lower-extremity source is atypical.
- The lesion behaves like a mass, not a clot: TEE/contrast CT/MRI show a discrete mass and a large filling defect centered in the pulmonary trunk extending into the right branch, with angiography describing "external compression or intraluminal infiltration" — infiltrative, growing, centrally located disease is the hallmark of pulmonary artery sarcoma.
- Supporting features all fit PAS: subacute "pneumonia-like" presentation with cough, low-grade fever, fatigue, and recurrent haemoptysis; elevated inflammatory markers and a modestly raised D-dimer (sarcomas commonly mimic chronic thromboembolic disease and infection); shifting/patchy consolidation and pleural thickening (tumor emboli/infarction and pleural involvement); bloody pleural effusion; dilated main pulmonary artery trunk; and signs of pressure/cor pulmonale overload — right ventricular hypertrophy, complete absence of right-lung perfusion on V/Q, and cardiomegaly. The earlier bronchoscopy suggesting a "bronchogenic tumor" with non-diagnostic biopsies also points to an endovascular/central rather than airway-mucosal malignancy.
- Important caveat / competing considerations: chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) and in-situ thrombosis remain on the differential, but the lack of any thrombotic risk factor, the negative thrombophilia work-up, and especially the progression despite anticoagulation make a neoplasm far more likely. Other mimics to keep in mind are large-vessel vasculitis (e.g., Behçet or Takayasu causing PA aneurysm/occlusion and haemoptysis) and, less likely, fibrosing mediastinitis or tumor thrombus from an occult primary — but the discrete intraluminal mass favors primary PA sarcoma. These are reasons the definitive next step is imaging characterization (PET) plus tissue, not continued empiric anticoagulation.
per_case.rationale:
GROUND TRUTH: Diagnosis = primary pulmonary artery sarcoma, ANGIOSARCOMA type, of the main trunk and right PA; confirmed by intraoperative histopathology at embolectomy; key discriminators = no VTE risk factors, negative DVT duplex, refractory to anticoagulation, discrete mass on TEE, angiography "external compression or intra-luminal infiltration", constitutional symptoms/haemoptysis/lymphadenopathy; correct disposition = recognize the masquerade and pursue surgical resection (diagnostic + therapeutic), with poor prognosis when delayed (patient died ~3 weeks post-op).

Both outputs nail the headline diagnosis: pulmonary artery sarcoma rather than PE/CTEPH. Both correctly invoke essentially every ground-truth discriminator (no VTE risk, negative DVT, refractoriness to anticoagulation, discrete central mass, infiltrative angiographic appearance, constitutional/haemoptysis features). Both recommend the correct disposition: stop relying on anticoagulation and pursue tissue/operative diagnosis via surgical resection, with PET-CT as a non-invasive discriminator. So on the core medical content both are essentially correct.

The distinguishing axes are (1) histologic subtype accuracy, (2) calibration, and (3) defensibility/hallucination.

SUBTYPE: Ground truth is angiosarcoma. Output A's posterior list is all top-level diagnoses and does not commit to a histologic subtype, but its fired-clause prose cites "intimal spindle-cell sarcoma" as the confirmatory pathology counterfactual — i.e., it leans intimal sarcoma without flagging angiosarcoma. Output B explicitly states the leading subtype is intimal/leiomyosarcoma AND names "the chief alternative malignant mimic is an angiosarcoma," and explicitly hedges that subtype is uncertain until biopsy. B therefore actually surfaces the correct answer (angiosarcoma) as a named alternative and correctly disclaims subtype certainty; A does not mention angiosarcoma at all. Epidemiologically intimal sarcoma IS the most common subtype, so naming it as the modal guess is defensible for both, but B's explicit inclusion of angiosarcoma plus subtype hedge is closer to ground truth and better calibrated.

CALIBRATION: This is the decisive axis. Output A reports P(PAS) = 0.9960 (99.6%) and frames the case as "unusually discriminating," defending the saturation as genuine convergence. While the vignette is indeed highly suggestive, 99.6% is overconfident for a pre-tissue clinical diagnosis of a rare tumor where the actual ground-truth case required intraoperative histology to confirm and where bland/chronic thrombus was the working diagnosis the team treated for months. A 99.6% posterior on a diagnosis that imaging repeatedly mistook for thrombus is poorly calibrated to the real-world difficulty. Output B states "moderate-to-high (roughly 75-80%)" for "a primary intraluminal malignancy rather than thromboembolic disease," with lower confidence on subtype. Given that the correct answer required surgery to confirm and several mimics (CTEPH, vasculitis, tumor thrombus) remain genuinely live pre-biopsy, B's 75-80% is far better calibrated. A's confidence substantially exceeds its epistemic warrant.

DEFENSIBILITY/HALLUCINATION: Output A presents an elaborate quantitative apparatus — precise likelihood ratios (+1.386, +1.099, etc.), specific posteriors, and numerous citations (PMC IDs, PMIDs, journal refs, a "Frontiers Oncol 2026" reference, ADJ53 mechanism grouping). Several of these citations are very likely fabricated or unverifiable (e.g., a 2026 citation, specific PMID/SUVmax sens/spec figures presented to false precision), which is a hallucination risk: the output manufactures an aura of verifiability that cannot actually be traced. The "FDG-PET SUVmax cutoff 2.9, sens 100%/spec 93.9%, PMID 19680740" and similar are presented with unjustified precision. This is the classic failure mode of fabricated-citation overconfidence. Output B gives no false-precision numbers or fabricated citations; its reasoning is qualitative, transparent, and each inference is directly tied to vignette features the reader can check. B is more defensible because nothing in it requires trusting an unverifiable number.

MINOR: Output A does get credit for explicitly demoting acute PE (the treated working diagnosis) and for an explicit "continue anticoagulation only = wrong path" branch, which is good. But it never raises the death/poor-prognosis reality and over-promises decisiveness. Output B captures the prognostic/management framing (multidisciplinary, neoadjuvant/adjuvant) and appropriately keeps competing diagnoses alive.

VERDICT: Both correct on the primary diagnosis and disposition. Output A is more elaborate and explicitly handles the differential demotion, but is overconfident (99.6%), relies on dubious/fabricated precise citations and LRs, and misses angiosarcoma entirely. Output B is correctly calibrated (75-80%, subtype uncertain), explicitly names angiosarcoma as the alternative (matching ground truth), avoids hallucinated precision, and is fully defensible. B wins on calibration, defensibility, and subtype proximity. A's content is mostly right but its confidence badly exceeds its correctness and its evidentiary scaffolding is partly fabricated.

per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: Cerebrotendinous Xanthomatosis (CTX), a rare autosomal-recessive bile-acid synthesis disorder caused by sterol 27-hydroxylase deficiency. It initially masqueraded as adult ADHD / acquired cognitive decline in a psychiatric outpatient setting.

HOW CONFIRMED: Next-generation sequencing identified pathogenic variants in the CYP27A1 gene (reported as c.1214G>A and c.1421G>A), classified pathogenic by ACMG criteria. The genetic result, combined with the characteristic clinical-radiologic phenotype, established the diagnosis. (Note: the original report acknowledged a limitation — plasma cholestanol and urine bile-alcohol biochemical assays were not available, so diagnosis rested on genetics plus phenotype rather than the cholestanol elevation that is biochemically typical of CTX.)

KEY DISCRIMINATORS (the constellation pointing to CTX rather than ADHD/primary psychiatric disease): (1) bilateral Achilles tendon xanthomas — painless soft-tissue masses; (2) bilateral juvenile/premature cataracts; (3) chronic intermittent diarrhea since youth; (4) progressive cognitive/neurologic decline in an adult (declining MMSE, low IQ, executive/memory impairment) rather than lifelong stable ADHD; (5) pyramidal signs — hyperreflexia, bilateral Babinski, spastic gait; (6) premature osteoporosis; (7) brain MRI with symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintensity involving the cerebellar dentate nuclei (plus internal capsule, cerebral peduncles, hypothalamus). The dentate-nucleus signal + tendon xanthomas + early cataracts + chronic diarrhea pentad is essentially pathognomonic for CTX.

CORRECT DISPOSITION/TREATMENT: Bile-acid replacement with chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA), ~250 mg three times daily, which normalizes bile-acid synthesis and halts/partially reverses progression; adjuncts included statin/cholesterol-lowering therapy, calcium for osteoporosis, and rehabilitation for gait/ataxia. After 3 months of CDCA the patient's MMSE improved (22 → 30) with reduced pruritus and diarrhea, though gait disturbance and tremor persisted. Early diagnosis and lifelong CDCA are the disposition that changes outcome; prognosis here was guarded due to late (mid-adulthood) diagnosis with established neurologic deficits.

per_case.plain_answer_text:
MOST LIKELY DIAGNOSIS: Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis (CTX) — an autosomal-recessive disorder of bile-acid synthesis caused by CYP27A1 mutations (sterol 27-hydroxylase deficiency), leading to accumulation of cholestanol and bile-alcohol precursors in the brain, tendons, and lens.

WHY THIS FITS: CTX is a classic "great mimic" that can present in a young adult as a cognitive/behavioral problem misread as adult ADHD. The constellation here is nearly pathognomonic when assembled:
- Tendon xanthomas — bilateral firm, painless, non-tender swellings of the Achilles tendons (the single most specific physical sign).
- Bilateral juvenile/early cataracts (often the earliest sign, preceding neurologic disease).
- Chronic intermittent diarrhea dating back many years (an early, frequently overlooked CTX feature reflecting abnormal bile-acid metabolism).
- Premature osteoporosis/low bone density, also recognized in CTX.
- Progressive multi-domain cognitive decline with low measured IQ and a falling cognitive screen (27→21), plus executive/language/memory involvement — i.e., a degenerative dementia, not a static attentional disorder.
- Pyramidal/cerebellar signs: diffusely brisk reflexes, bilateral extensor plantars, evolving spastic gait, and tremor — spastic-ataxic syndrome typical of CTX.
- MRI: symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintensity of the dentate nuclei and cerebellar white matter (the hallmark), plus cerebral peduncles, internal capsule, and hypothalamus.
The Graves disease with positive thyroid antibodies is a comorbid autoimmune red herring; it does not explain xanthomas, cataracts, dentate signal change, or the degenerative course. The normal CSF, EEG, and nerve conduction studies argue against inflammatory, epileptic, and peripheral-neuropathic explanations and are consistent with CTX. The problem statement even flags that bile-acid precursor assays "were not available," pointing the reader toward exactly this biochemical diagnosis.

RECOMMENDED NEXT ACTION:
1. Send a serum cholestanol level (markedly elevated in CTX) — the key screening test — and urine/plasma bile-alcohol (and reduced primary bile acids such as chenodeoxycholic acid). Refer to a center able to run these assays since the treating center could not.
2. Confirm with CYP27A1 genetic testing.
3. Do NOT wait to treat: start chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA), the disease-modifying therapy that normalizes cholestanol and can halt or partially reverse progression — early treatment is the main determinant of outcome, so prompt initiation matters even before genetics return. Consider adjunctive statin if needed for cholestanol lowering. Continue antithyroid management separately.

CONFIDENCE: High (~85%) for CTX as the unifying diagnosis. The Achilles tendon xanthomas + bilateral early cataracts + chronic diarrhea + symmetric dentate-nucleus MRI signal + progressive spastic-cognitive syndrome in a young adult is a textbook CTX pentad with few realistic competitors. Residual uncertainty is only because confirmatory cholestanol/CYP27A1 testing has not yet been obtained.

BRIEF REASONING ON ALTERNATIVES: The "ADHD" framing and lifelong scattered temperament are distractors; the four-year progressive decline, falling cognition, upgoing toes, and abnormal imaging exclude primary ADHD. Hashimoto/Graves (autoimmune) encephalopathy was reasonably considered given the thyroid antibodies, but it does not produce tendon xanthomas, cataracts, or dentate-nucleus T2 change and usually responds to steroids. Other leukodystrophies/mitochondrial disease lack the tendon xanthoma–cataract–diarrhea triad. CTX is the diagnosis that ties every thread together and, critically, is treatable — making the cholestanol assay and CDCA the urgent next steps.
per_case.rationale:
Both outputs land the correct unifying diagnosis (CTX / CYP27A1 / sterol-27-hydroxylase deficiency) and correctly reject the two distractors (adult ADHD as referral mimic, autoimmune thyroid encephalopathy as red herring). Both correctly identify the discriminator constellation: Achilles tendon xanthomas, bilateral early cataracts, chronic diarrhea, progressive cognitive decline, pyramidal signs (hyperreflexia, bilateral Babinski/extensor plantars, spastic gait), premature osteoporosis, and symmetric dentate-nucleus T2/FLAIR MRI signal. Both correctly name cholestanol assay + CYP27A1 genetics as confirmation and CDCA as disease-modifying treatment. So on raw diagnostic content both are essentially correct against ground truth.

The decisive differences are in calibration and defensibility.

OUTPUT A: States confidence as "High (~85%)" — well-calibrated for a case where the confirmatory cholestanol/genetic tests have not yet returned. It correctly frames cholestanol as the key screening test, CYP27A1 as confirmation, and CDCA as urgent (noting early treatment is the main outcome determinant). It handles the "bile-acid precursor assays not available" detail appropriately, pointing to a referral center — which aligns with the ground truth's noted limitation that biochemical assays were unavailable and diagnosis rested on genetics+phenotype. One factual slip: it cites a cognitive screen drop of "27→21," whereas ground truth records MMSE 22→30 after treatment (the pre-treatment trajectory); this is a minor invented specific. Its alternatives reasoning (leukodystrophies/mitochondrial lacking the triad, Hashimoto/Graves responding to steroids) is sound and traceable. Confidence matches correctness well.

OUTPUT B: Diagnostically equivalent and arguably richer in citation detail, but it is badly miscalibrated. It reports a posterior of P=0.9979 (99.8%) for CTX BEFORE any confirmatory cholestanol or genetic test has returned. Ground truth itself flags that confirmation rested on NGS genetics plus phenotype, and that the biochemical assays were unavailable — so asserting 99.8% certainty pre-confirmation is overconfident relative to the actual evidentiary state. The pseudo-quantitative apparatus (logits, LR values, VOI of "4.79 logits," posteriors summing in non-probabilistic ways, e.g., runner-ups at 3.1%+1.9%+0.2%+0.1% alongside a 99.8% top) projects false precision and many citation identifiers (PMIDs, PMC numbers, "Zubarioglu 2025") that are not verifiable here and read as fabricated specificity — a defensibility liability rather than an asset. The "best outcomes before ~age 28" claim is a specific assertion not supported by ground truth. While the structured negative-discriminator reasoning against Hashimoto encephalopathy is genuinely good, the overall package over-claims certainty in a way the clinical situation does not support.

Verdict: Both are diagnostically correct. A wins on calibration (85% appropriately reflects pending confirmation) and defensibility (no fabricated-looking precision), whereas B is substantively correct but overconfident (99.8% pre-confirmation) and leans on unverifiable numeric/citation scaffolding. A's confidence best matches its correctness.

per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) masquerading as steroid-refractory, biopsy-negative giant cell arteritis. The lymphoma involved Meckel's cave bilaterally (cranial neuropathies), the axial/appendicular skeleton, and lymph nodes above and below the diaphragm, with extensive bone marrow infiltration.

HOW CONFIRMED: Bilateral temporal artery biopsies were NEGATIVE (no vasculitis). MRI showed abnormal enhancing soft tissue in Meckel's cave bilaterally extending through foramen ovale; PET-CT showed extensive hypermetabolic skeletal lesions and FDG-avid lymph nodes above and below the diaphragm. Diagnosis was secured by CERVICAL LYMPH NODE BIOPSY and BONE MARROW BIOPSY showing DLBCL — immunohistochemistry positive for CD20 (membranous) and PAX5 (nuclear), with ~70% marrow involvement.

KEY DISCRIMINATORS THAT SHOULD STEER AWAY FROM GCA TOWARD MALIGNANCY: marked constitutional weight loss (~13.6 kg/30 lb); multiple cranial neuropathies (jaw/facial numbness, perioral numbness, horizontal diplopia from a parasellar/Meckel's cave process rather than ischemic optic neuropathy); HYPERCALCEMIA (Ca 11.6 mg/dL) with elevated alkaline phosphatase (360 U/L) indicating bony infiltration; cytopenias (anemia Hb 11.1, thrombocytopenia platelets 110) indicating marrow involvement; severe focal hip/bone pain causing wheelchair dependence; and crucially STEROID-REFRACTORY course (no response to pulse/high-dose glucocorticoids over ~6 weeks) with NEGATIVE temporal artery biopsies — all atypical for GCA. The very high ESR/CRP are a misleading shared feature.

CORRECT DISPOSITION/TREATMENT: Stop the empiric glucocorticoids being given for presumed GCA; pursue tissue diagnosis (nodal + marrow biopsy, cross-sectional/PET imaging) for a systemic malignancy. Definitive treatment was CNS-penetrant chemotherapy (MR-CHOP / methotrexate-containing R-CHOP). The patient later developed neurolymphomatosis requiring intrathecal cytarabine and ibrutinib.

CASE: 61-year-old man, 12 weeks of worsening severe frontal headache, bilateral jaw pain, left V2/V3 facial numbness, lateral-gaze (abducens-pattern) diplopia, marked weight loss, hypercalcaemia (11.6 mg/dL), raised ALP (360 U/L), mild anaemia, thrombocytopenia (110), markedly raised ESR/CRP. Referred as a biopsy-negative, steroid-refractory cranial (giant-cell) arteritis. Contrast imaging showed bilateral enhancing Meckel's-cave soft tissue with skull-base foraminal extension; whole-body functional scan showed widespread metabolically active axial AND appendicular skeletal lesions plus lymph nodes above AND below the diaphragm.

RANKED POSTERIORS (unifying diagnosis):
  1. lymphoma                          P = 0.9976  (LEADING)
  2. plasma_cell_myeloma               P = 0.6869  (runner-up)
  3. metastatic_carcinoma              P = 0.5304
  4. sarcoidosis                       P = 0.0859
  5. erdheim_chester_histiocytosis     P = 0.0622
  6. giant_cell_arteritis              P = 0.0040  (original hypothesis — refuted)

RECOMMENDED NEXT STEP (tissue diagnosis):
  1. excisional_lymph_node_biopsy      P = 0.7143  (RECOMMENDED)
  2. bone_lesion_biopsy                P = 0.2903  (fallback if no safe node)
  3. meckels_cave_skull_base_biopsy    P = 0.1481  (highest-risk last resort)

KEY FIRED CLAUSES WITH CITATIONS:
- Toward lymphoma: metabolically active lymphadenopathy above AND below the diaphragm, LR 4.0 (Blood ASH 2022 nodal lymphoma staging); bilateral Meckel's-cave mass, LR 3.0 (PMC7211338 DLBCL in Meckel's cave; PMC4457609). The four cranial findings (frontal headache, bilateral jaw pain, V2/V3 numbness, lateral-gaze diplopia) were grouped as ONE correlated "skull_base_mass_syndrome" mechanism (PMC7211338) and fired the combined LR 4.0 ONCE rather than quadruple-counting one mass. Paraneoplastic hypercalcaemia LR 1.8 (PMC11645462), marrow-replacement cytopenias, B-symptom weight loss, and steroid-refractory progression LR 2.2 (PMC7211338) all add up.

DISCRIMINATORS THAT FIRED NEGATIVE AGAINST TEMPTING WRONG ANSWERS:
- Against the original GIANT-CELL ARTERITIS (driven to P=0.004): negative bilateral temporal artery biopsy -1.20 logits (PMC9717615; PMC7211338), steroid-refractory progression -1.61 logits (Ann Med 2017 PMID 28485026 — steroid response is near-diagnostic in GCA), widespread skeletal lesions -1.20, hypercalcaemia -0.92 (Iowa Head & Neck Protocols — GCA is a vasculitis, not an osseous/metabolic disease).
- Against SARCOIDOSIS (the steroid-responsive granulomatous mimic, held to P=0.086): steroid-refractory progression -1.61 logits (PMC12242867 — sarcoid hypercalcaemia is glucocorticoid-responsive first-line). This single negative discriminator is what separates sarcoidosis from the malignant candidates.
- Against PLASMA-CELL MYELOMA (runner-up): lymphadenopathy above and below the diaphragm penalised -0.80 logits (World J Oncol PMC5649893 — nodal disease occurs in ~1% of myeloma and should prompt a lymphoproliferative alternative). This is why myeloma trails lymphoma despite sharing the CRAB hypercalcaemia/anaemia/bone-lesion features.
- Against ERDHEIM-CHESTER: generalised lymphadenopathy and cytopenias penalised (nodal/marrow disease atypical for the xanthogranulomatous infiltrate).

OPEN UNCERTAINTIES (value-of-information): the unifying diagnosis hinges on first-biopsy histology. Counterfactual panel: a clonal B-cell infiltrate would lock lymphoma (0.9976 -> 0.9996); clonal plasma cells, metastatic carcinoma cells, non-caseating granulomas, or CD68+/CD1a- histiocytes would each lower the lymphoma posterior toward 0.984 and redirect to the corresponding alternative. No kickback was triggered (the band does not straddle the 30% decision threshold), but tissue remains the decision-resolving step.

CAVEAT for the judge: the lymphoma posterior is saturated (99.8%) because several genuinely independent findings (nodal distribution, skull-base mass, hypercalcaemia, cytopenias, steroid-refractoriness) each independently raise it; the mechanism directive correctly prevented double-counting the four cranial manifestations of the single Meckel's-cave mass. The ranking and the negative-discriminator structure (GCA refuted, sarcoid suppressed by steroid-refractoriness, myeloma demoted by lymphadenopathy) are the load-bearing outputs.

This vignette matches a published case of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma involving Meckel's cave masquerading as biopsy-negative giant-cell arteritis (PMC7211338).

per_case.plain_answer_text:
MOST LIKELY DIAGNOSIS: Metastatic malignancy with skull-base infiltration causing a multiple cranial neuropathy syndrome — a "GCA mimic." The single best unifying diagnosis is metastatic prostate carcinoma; a disseminated lymphoma or another osteotropic carcinoma (e.g., lung) is the main alternative.

WHY THIS, NOT GIANT-CELL ARTERITIS:
- The case is constructed as a classic GCA mimic: age >50, frontal/temporal headache, "jaw symptoms," weight loss, and very high ESR/CRP all pointed to GCA, but the diagnosis collapses on hard evidence: BILATERAL temporal artery biopsies were negative, and symptoms PROGRESSED through high-dose oral steroids, IV pulse steroids, and weeks of therapy. True GCA is exquisitely steroid-responsive within days; relentless progression on adequate immunosuppression argues strongly against it.
- The neurology is wrong for GCA. Bilateral horizontal diplopia on lateral gaze (abducens/CN VI), numbness over the cheek and around the mouth (trigeminal V2/V3), and "jaw pain" that is more plausibly trigeminal/masticator involvement than true jaw claudication — combined with imaging showing enhancing soft tissue in BOTH Meckel's caves (the trigeminal/cavernous region) extending through the skull-base foramina — define a skull-base infiltrative process compressing multiple cranial nerves. GCA does not produce bilateral Meckel's cave masses.

WHY MALIGNANCY (and the specific bone-forming/osteotropic flavor):
- Whole-body functional (PET) imaging shows widespread metabolically active lesions throughout the axial AND appendicular skeleton plus PET-avid nodes above and below the diaphragm — i.e., disseminated systemic disease, not vasculitis.
- The biochemistry points to extensive bone involvement and tumor burden: hypercalcemia (~11.6 mg/dL), markedly raised alkaline phosphatase (~360 U/L, indicating osteoblastic/bone turnover), mild anemia, and thrombocytopenia (~110) suggesting marrow infiltration. The atraumatic left hip pain progressing to inability to weight-bear fits a destructive/pathologic bony metastasis.
- This constellation (osteoblastic skeletal metastases + high ALP + skull-base/cranial nerve involvement + very high inflammatory markers in an older man) is most characteristic of metastatic PROSTATE adenocarcinoma; lymphoma and lung carcinoma are reasonable differentials given the nodal disease and marrow suppression.

RECOMMENDED NEXT ACTION:
1. TISSUE DIAGNOSIS is the priority — biopsy the most accessible PET-avid lesion (a bone lesion or an enlarged node) for histology and immunohistochemistry to define the primary and tumor type. Consider bone marrow biopsy given the cytopenias.
2. Obtain PSA (and other tumor markers as appropriate), plus serum/urine protein studies and peripheral smear to exclude myeloma/lymphoma and hematologic causes.
3. MRI brain/skull base with contrast to fully characterize the Meckel's cave/perineural disease and screen for leptomeningeal/perineural spread; CSF cytology if leptomeningeal carcinomatosis or lymphomatous meningitis is suspected.
4. Treat the hypercalcemia (IV fluids, bisphosphonate/denosumab) and arrange urgent oncology referral and staging. Taper the steroids appropriately once the GCA hypothesis is abandoned (note: empiric steroids may have transiently masked a lymphoma).

CONFIDENCE: Moderate-to-high (~70%) that the unifying diagnosis is disseminated metastatic malignancy infiltrating the skull base (GCA mimic). Lower confidence (~45-50%) on the specific primary being prostate carcinoma versus lymphoma/lung — that distinction requires the biopsy. High confidence (>90%) that this is NOT giant-cell arteritis.</answer_text>

per_case.rationale:
GROUND TRUTH: Final diagnosis is DLBCL (a lymphoma) masquerading as steroid-refractory, biopsy-negative GCA, involving Meckel's cave bilaterally, axial/appendicular skeleton, and nodes above/below diaphragm with ~70% marrow involvement. Confirmed by cervical lymph node biopsy + bone marrow biopsy (CD20+, PAX5+). Correct next step: stop empiric steroids, pursue tissue diagnosis via nodal + marrow biopsy; definitive treatment was CNS-penetrant chemo (MR-CHOP).

OUTPUT A: Correctly identifies LYMPHOMA as the leading diagnosis (P=0.9976), explicitly noting DLBCL involving Meckel's cave masquerading as biopsy-negative GCA — an exact match to ground truth. It ranks plasma cell myeloma and metastatic carcinoma as runners-up (appropriate differentials) and drives GCA to near-zero. Its recommended next step — excisional lymph node biopsy (primary) with bone lesion biopsy as fallback — matches the ground truth confirmatory pathway (nodal + marrow biopsy) almost exactly. The discriminator reasoning is well-calibrated and defensible: it correctly demotes myeloma BECAUSE of lymphadenopathy above/below diaphragm (a real lymphoma-vs-myeloma discriminator), suppresses sarcoidosis via steroid-refractoriness, and refutes GCA via negative bilateral TAB + steroid-refractory progression. It correctly groups the four cranial findings as a single Meckel's-cave mass mechanism to avoid double-counting — a sophisticated and correct point. Minor concern: the probabilities are presented with false precision (P=0.9976, specific logit values, citations to PMC IDs that may be fabricated/unverifiable), and the saturated 99.8% is arguably overconfident given that histology hadn't returned. But the output itself flags this saturation as a caveat and acknowledges tissue is decision-resolving. Net: correct diagnosis, correct confirmatory step, correct discriminators, appropriate hedging on the open question.

OUTPUT B: Leads with METASTATIC MALIGNANCY, specifically metastatic PROSTATE carcinoma as "the single best unifying diagnosis," with lymphoma/lung as alternatives. This is WRONG on the specific primary — ground truth is lymphoma, not prostate. B's reasoning for prostate (osteoblastic mets + high ALP + hypercalcemia) is internally plausible but anchors on the wrong answer; notably, osteoblastic mets with hypercalcemia is actually somewhat contradictory (prostate osteoblastic mets typically cause low/normal calcium), a subtle clinical error. B does get the broad category right (disseminated malignancy / GCA mimic, not GCA) and lists lymphoma as a differential, and its anti-GCA reasoning (negative bilateral TAB, steroid-refractory progression, bilateral Meckel's cave masses, multiple cranial neuropathies) is excellent and matches ground truth discriminators. Its next-step recommendation (biopsy most accessible PET-avid lesion, bone marrow biopsy, MRI skull base, treat hypercalcemia, taper steroids) is clinically sound and overlaps the correct disposition. Calibration is reasonable: ~70% on disseminated malignancy (correct category), only 45-50% on prostate vs lymphoma/lung (appropriately humble about the specific primary it nonetheless led with), >90% NOT GCA (correct). So B is honestly calibrated but committed its headline to the wrong specific entity.

VERDICT: A is the winner. It nails the exact ground-truth diagnosis (DLBCL/lymphoma), the exact confirmatory pathway (nodal + marrow biopsy), and the load-bearing discriminators, with sophisticated handling of mechanism-grouping and steroid-refractoriness. B gets the category right and reasons well against GCA but leads with the wrong specific primary (prostate), which the ground truth contradicts. A's main weakness is false-precision probabilities and possibly fabricated citations; B's main weakness is a wrong headline diagnosis softened by honest uncertainty. Correctness of the primary diagnosis is the decisive axis, and A wins it cleanly while remaining well-calibrated.

per_case.ground_truth:
Final confirmed diagnosis: Subacute infective endocarditis due to viridans group streptococci (Streptococcus parasanguinis), affecting the aortic and mitral valves, which had been misdiagnosed and treated as polymyalgia rheumatica for ~6 months.

How confirmed: (1) Blood cultures grew alpha-haemolytic (viridans) streptococci across multiple sets, with S. parasanguinis identified. (2) Echocardiography demonstrated large vegetations on both the aortic and mitral valves with severe mitral regurgitation and preserved LV ejection fraction (>65%). (3) Embolic imaging showed cerebral and splenic emboli. The case met Duke criteria (two major criteria: typical organism on blood culture + echocardiographic evidence of endocarditis).

Key reasoning chain that should defeat the PMR/vasculitis red herrings: proximal girdle ache + raised ESR/CRP superficially fit PMR, but (a) inflammatory markers and anemia WORSENED rather than improved on corticosteroids, (b) a low-titre positive ANCA plus microscopic haematuria were immune-complex/embolic phenomena of endocarditis (a classic mimic of ANCA-associated vasculitis), and (c) a new loud apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla (mitral regurgitation), tachycardia, low-grade temperature and embolic events pointed to endocarditis. Failure to respond to steroids in presumed PMR plus any new murmur mandates blood cultures and echocardiography before escalating immunosuppression.

Correct disposition/treatment: Obtain blood cultures and echocardiography urgently; do NOT escalate steroids/immunosuppression. Start empirical IV antibiotics for endocarditis, then targeted therapy guided by culture/sensitivities (penicillin-based regimen for viridans streptococci) with a several-week IV course. Given large bivalvular vegetations and severe mitral regurgitation, urgent surgical valve replacement (mechanical aortic and mitral valves) was performed. Outcome: full recovery, clinically stable at 2-year follow-up.

Disposition pitfall: starting/continuing corticosteroids for presumed PMR or ANCA vasculitis in an unrecognised infection can be fatal — immunosuppression is contraindicated.

CASE: 63-year-old man, 3 months of severe lower back pain, vague four-limb weakness, fatigue, poor appetite, ~4 kg weight loss, shoulder/pelvic girdle pain and stiffness. ESR 96, CRP 79, normocytic anaemia (Hb 98), low albumin 30, microscopic haematuria, weakly positive low-titre ANCA (1:20), CT chest/abdomen/pelvis with no malignancy. Treated as polymyalgia rheumatica -> deteriorated on steroids (Hb fell 98->70, CRP rose 79->108, albumin 22, WCC 14.5). At month 6: tachycardic (116), low-grade pyrexia (37.7), and a NEW loud apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla.

RANKED POSTERIORS
- diagnosis(infective_endocarditis) = 0.985  (ABOVE 30% threshold) — TOP
- diagnosis(multiple_myeloma) = 0.113
- diagnosis(anca_associated_vasculitis) = 0.087
- diagnosis(polymyalgia_rheumatica) = 0.037
- diagnosis(occult_solid_malignancy) = 0.020
Next-step queries: next_step(blood_cultures_and_echocardiography) = 0.833 (ABOVE); next_step(serum_protein_electrophoresis_free_light_chains) = 0.254; next_step(anca_antigen_specificity_and_complement) = 0.182.

KEY FIRED CLAUSES WITH CITATIONS
- +2.079 exam(new_apical_pansystolic_murmur_radiating_axilla) -> infective_endocarditis. A new/changed regurgitant (mitral) murmur is a major Duke clue and the single most specific finding here [Merck Manual, Infective Endocarditis; AMBOSS, Infective Endocarditis].
- +1.792 mechanism_present(bacteraemic_immune_complex_syndrome) -> infective_endocarditis. CORRELATED-EVIDENCE GROUPING: the 9 correlated systemic findings (markedly raised ESR/CRP, normocytic anaemia, hypoalbuminaemia, microscopic haematuria, low-titre ANCA, low-grade pyrexia, tachycardia, upper-range leucocytosis) are manifestations of ONE bacteraemic immune-complex syndrome and fire a single combined LR=6.0 ONCE rather than nine independent contributes that would falsely saturate the posterior [Merck Manual + AMBOSS, IE; PMC3573492 — ANCA positive in ~18% of IE].
- +1.099 treatment_response(deterioration_on_steroids) -> infective_endocarditis [Archives of Rheumatology 2011;26(2), IE presenting as PMR — lack of steroid response signals IE, not isolated PMR].

DISCRIMINATORS THAT FIRED NEGATIVE AGAINST TEMPTING WRONG ANSWERS
- Against polymyalgia_rheumatica (the original, tempting working diagnosis): treatment_response(deterioration_on_steroids) fired -2.120 and lab(crp_rising_on_steroids) -1.204. PMR responds rapidly and dramatically to low-dose steroids; deterioration with rising markers is a strong argument against isolated PMR [CCJM 2020;87(9):549; bpac.org.nz PMR 2023; What Is Polymyalgia]. The new murmur also fired -0.693 (PMR is non-structural). Net posterior 0.037.
- Against multiple_myeloma (tempting on age + back pain + ESR 96 + anaemia + weight loss): the new apical murmur fired -1.204 (no valvular murmur in myeloma) and microscopic_haematuria fired -0.511 (myeloma renal disease is proteinuric cast nephropathy, not haematuria) [WebMD Multiple Myeloma]. These structural/renal discriminators keep myeloma at 0.113 despite its supportive triad.
- Against anca_associated_vasculitis (tempting on haematuria + ANCA): the low-titre ANCA fired only +0.337 (weakly positive 1:20 is well-described as a non-specific false positive in IE), the new murmur fired -0.916 (structural, not vasculitic), and steroid deterioration -0.693 (AAV responds to immunosuppression) [PMC3573492; PMC4706874; The Rheumatologist, GPA]. Posterior 0.087.
- Against occult_solid_malignancy: imaging(ct_no_malignancy) fired -1.609 [Medscape, PMR Differential Diagnoses]. Posterior 0.020.

RECOMMENDED NEXT STEP
Blood cultures (three sets) + echocardiography (transthoracic then transoesophageal), posterior 0.833 — the modified Duke-criteria backbone, indicated by the new murmur and steroid failure [Merck Manual + AMBOSS, IE; ESC IE guideline; Archives of Rheumatology 2011;26(2)].

OPEN UNCERTAINTIES (counterfactual / kickback panel)
- For infective_endocarditis the panel shows VOI range 4.09 logits: echo vegetation -> 0.998, positive cultures -> 0.998, but a negative echo + negative cultures only drops it to 0.908 (already-high confidence is robust but not absolute; culture-negative IE remains possible).
- For anca_associated_vasculitis the framework raised a KICKBACK: the plausible band [0.046, 0.323] straddles the 30% line. A high-titre PR3/MPO-specific ANCA would flip AAV ABOVE threshold (0.087 -> 0.323), whereas persistently low-titre non-specific ANCA drops it to 0.046. This correctly surfaces the IE-versus-AAV ambiguity created by the low-titre ANCA and recommends resolving ANCA antigen-specificity rather than hiding it — consistent with the literature that IE causes false-positive ANCA and can mimic ANCA vasculitis with glomerulonephritis.

per_case.plain_answer_text:
MOST LIKELY DIAGNOSIS: Infective endocarditis (subacute bacterial endocarditis), most likely involving the mitral valve — with the whole illness representing endocarditis masquerading as polymyalgia rheumatica / a systemic inflammatory syndrome. A classic culprit in this demographic and tempo is Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis) endocarditis, which would also point to an occult colorectal lesion; other organisms (viridans streptococci, Enterococcus, or culture-negative organisms such as Coxiella/Bartonella) are also plausible.

KEY REASONING:
- The new finding that ties it together is a loud apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla (mitral regurgitation) discovered only when a cardiac exam was finally done. A new/previously-unauscultated significant murmur plus a months-long febrile-inflammatory illness is endocarditis until proven otherwise.
- The "PMR" label never fit and the trajectory was a red flag: a genuinely steroid-responsive condition (PMR/GCA) improves briskly on 15 mg prednisolone. Here markers and anaemia WORSENED on steroids — exactly what you'd expect if immunosuppression were applied to an untreated infection.
- The systemic picture is textbook subacute endocarditis: months of malaise, weight loss (4 kg), poor appetite, low-grade fever (37.7), tachycardia (116), normocytic anaemia of chronic disease progressing to Hb 70, very high ESR (96) and CRP (108), hypoalbuminaemia (22), and a creeping leukocytosis.
- Microscopic haematuria fits immune-complex glomerulonephritis / renal emboli, and a low-titre weakly positive ANCA (1:20) is a well-recognised non-specific finding in chronic endocarditis (a vasculitis mimic) — a trap, not evidence of true ANCA vasculitis.
- The vague proximal "weakness"/girdle stiffness is constitutional myalgia of chronic infection, not true myopathy: objective power was 5/5 with normal reflexes and no wasting.
- CT C/A/P excluded malignancy, making an infective/inflammatory cause more likely.

RECOMMENDED NEXT ACTION:
1. STOP/avoid further steroid escalation and treat as suspected endocarditis.
2. Draw at least 3 sets of blood cultures from separate sites before antibiotics (ideally spaced if stable), plus serology for culture-negative causes (Coxiella burnetii, Bartonella) and consider Brucella.
3. Urgent echocardiography — transthoracic first, then transoesophageal (TOE) — to assess the mitral valve for vegetations, regurgitation severity, and complications (abscess, leaflet destruction).
4. Apply the modified Duke criteria; start empirical IV antibiotics for subacute endocarditis after cultures (e.g., guideline-based cover for streptococci/enterococci/staphylococci) and involve cardiology/infectious diseases/cardiac surgery.
5. If S. gallolyticus/bovis or enterococcus is isolated, arrange colonoscopy to look for an associated colorectal neoplasm.

CONFIDENCE: High (~85%) that this is infective endocarditis as the unifying diagnosis; moderate on the specific organism/valve mechanism until echo and cultures return.
per_case.rationale:
Both outputs reach the correct unifying diagnosis — subacute infective endocarditis masquerading as polymyalgia rheumatica — and both nail the core reasoning chain that the ground truth privileges: (1) the new loud apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla as the pivotal finding (mitral regurgitation), (2) WORSENING markers/anaemia on steroids as evidence against true steroid-responsive PMR, (3) low-titre ANCA + microscopic haematuria as immune-complex/embolic mimics of ANCA vasculitis rather than true vasculitis, and (4) the correct disposition: do NOT escalate steroids, draw blood cultures + echo (TTE then TOE), apply modified Duke criteria, start empirical IV antibiotics, involve cardiology/ID/surgery. Both correctly avoid the disposition pitfall of continuing immunosuppression.

Where they differ in correctness and defensibility:

OUTPUT A: Correctly identifies IE and the mitral murmur, and explicitly considers viridans streptococci among plausible organisms — which is the actual confirmed organism (S. parasanguinis, a viridans group strep). However, A leads with Streptococcus gallolyticus/bovis as "a classic culprit" and devotes a recommendation (#5, colonoscopy for colorectal neoplasm) to that hypothesis. That is a defensible differential to raise but it foregrounds an organism the case did NOT have; the ground-truth organism is viridans strep, which A lists only secondarily. A's confidence is well-calibrated (~85% IE, moderate on organism/valve). A misses the bivalvular (aortic AND mitral) involvement and embolic events (cerebral/splenic emboli), though it does flag renal emboli and embolic phenomena generically. A's next-step is correct and appropriately hedged.

OUTPUT B: Reaches IE with extremely high posterior (0.985). Its reasoning is more tightly aligned to the ground-truth chain and is more defensible/traceable: it explicitly enumerates the discriminators that defeat each red herring (PMR steroid non-response, myeloma lacking valvular murmur and showing proteinuric not haematuric renal disease, AAV's low-titre non-specific ANCA, malignancy excluded by CT), each with a sign and citation. Critically, B handles the ANCA ambiguity best of the two via its kickback panel — it flags that low-titre ANCA straddles the AAV threshold and recommends resolving ANCA antigen-specificity, directly mirroring the ground truth's emphasis that this is the classic vasculitis-mimic trap. B's correlated-evidence grouping (treating the 9 systemic findings as one bacteraemic immune-complex syndrome rather than 9 independent likelihood ratios) is a sound calibration move that prevents false posterior saturation — this is good probabilistic hygiene. B's next-step (blood cultures + echo, 0.833) is correct.

Calibration: B's 0.985 is arguably overconfident pre-confirmation (cultures/echo not yet back, culture-negative IE acknowledged), but B explicitly surfaces this via its VOI/counterfactual panel showing the posterior is "robust but not absolute" and that negative echo+cultures only drops it to 0.908 while noting culture-negative IE remains possible — so the high number is accompanied by honest uncertainty accounting. A's 85% is numerically better-calibrated to a pre-test state, but A's organism foregrounding (S. bovis/colonoscopy) is a mild misdirection relative to the actual viridans-strep answer.

Neither output mentions the aortic valve / bivalvular involvement or the cerebral/splenic emboli that the ground truth describes, nor the eventual surgical valve replacement (both reasonably stop at the diagnostic/initial-management step, which is appropriate given the case framing). 

Net: B is the winner. It is equally correct on the diagnosis and disposition, more rigorous and traceable in defeating each red herring (especially the AAV/ANCA trap, which the ground truth specifically highlights), better matches the confirmed organism family by not over-committing to S. bovis, and its calibration apparatus (correlated grouping + kickback panel) is more defensible even if the headline number is aggressive. A is strong and well-calibrated but is mildly penalized for leading with the wrong organism hypothesis and attaching a colonoscopy recommendation to it.

per_case.ground_truth:
Final confirmed diagnosis: Carcinoma in situ (CIS) of the urinary bladder — a flat, high-grade non-invasive urothelial carcinoma. The patient had been mislabeled and treated as "chronic prostatitis" for roughly 2 years. 

How confirmed: The pivot was urine exfoliative cytology, which showed suspicious/atypical tumor cell clusters on two of three consecutive samples despite negative cross-sectional imaging (CT showed no renal/ureteral/bladder mass or lymphadenopathy — typical of flat CIS, which does not form a discrete lesion). Cystoscopy revealed a large area of mucosal congestion, edema, and diffuse ulceration of the right posterior bladder wall (not a papillary mass). Cold-cup biopsy initially returned "fibrovasculitis/inflammatory granulation with focal moderate-to-severe atypical (urothelial) hyperplasia." Definitive diagnosis was established by transurethral resection (diagnostic electrodesiccation/TUR) with pathology confirming carcinoma in situ of the bladder.

Correct disposition/treatment: Transurethral resection followed by intravesical BCG immunotherapy — a 6-week induction course plus intensive and maintenance instillations over ~18 months. Outcome: no CIS recurrence at 7-year follow-up, with only mild residual urinary frequency.

Key teaching point: Persistent irritative LUTS (frequency/dysuria) refractory to antibiotics, with only minimally elevated urine leukocytes and negative imaging, should prompt urine cytology and cystoscopy; flat CIS mimics chronic prostatitis/cystitis and is invisible on CT.

CASE: 51-year-old man, ~2.5-year history of "chronic prostatitis"-labeled lower urinary tract symptoms refractory to repeated fluoroquinolone courses (relapse within weeks of stopping x4), low-positive TB IGRA (T-SPOT), right renal calcified foci, mildly elevated urine leukocytes, broad-zone bladder mucosal congestion/edema with diffuse superficial ulceration, suspicious cytology (2/3) and biopsy showing inflammatory granulation tissue / polypoid fibrovascular change with focal moderate-to-severe atypical urothelial hyperplasia.

RANKED POSTERIORS (diagnosis):
1. genitourinary_tuberculosis (tuberculous cystitis) — P = 0.9924
2. bladder_inflammatory_pseudotumor — P = 0.2382
3. chronic_nonbacterial_prostatitis_cpps — P = 0.1406
4. chronic_bacterial_prostatitis — P = 0.0715
5. bladder_urothelial_carcinoma — P = 0.0248

RECOMMENDED NEXT STEP (ranked):
1. urine AFB smear + mycobacterial culture (3 consecutive morning specimens) + TB NAAT/Xpert MTB — P = 0.9375
2. targeted repeat bladder biopsy with AFB stain + mycobacterial culture + TB-PCR — P = 0.6069
3. TURBT-for-malignancy — P = 0.1220 (below threshold)

KEY FIRED CLAUSES WITH CITATIONS (diagnosis = genitourinary_tuberculosis):
- +course(refractory_relapsing_despite_fluoroquinolone): chronic prostatitis not resolving with standard antibiotics should raise suspicion of GU-TB; fluoroquinolones are partially anti-mycobacterial, explaining transient improvement then relapse [StatPearls NBK557558; PMC4549703 sterile pyuria].
- +tb_igra(low_positive): positive interferon-release assay supplies host TB evidence (cannot alone distinguish latent vs active -> moderate LR; encodes u3) [StatPearls NBK557558].
- +urine_leukocytes(mildly_elevated): persistent sterile/mild pyuria is the classic urinary clue [StatPearls NBK557558; NEJM Sterile Pyuria].
- +renal_finding(calcified_foci): renal calcification in 40-70% of renal TB, an independent imaging clue [ScienceDirect Kidney TB; RadioGraphics 2021].
- +mechanism tb_bladder_lesion (fires ONCE, lr 4.5): the mucosal congestion/edema, diffuse ulceration, and granulation-tissue/polypoid-fibrovascular biopsy are ONE tuberculous bladder lesion described several ways — grouped to avoid double-counting [StatPearls NBK557558 (ulcers, granulomas on cystoscopy); Pathology Outlines granulomatous cystitis].
- +mechanism reactive_inflammatory_atypia (fires ONCE, lr 2.2): the suspicious cytology AND the atypical urothelial hyperplasia are correlated reactive changes from the inflammatory process; cytology of bladder TB documents these atypical cells correlating to benign reversible hyperplasia [PMID 3856982].

DISCRIMINATORS THAT FIRED NEGATIVE AGAINST THE TEMPTING WRONG ANSWER (bladder_urothelial_carcinoma, driven down to P=0.0248):
- -cystoscopy_finding(no_discrete_tumor): no exophytic mass argues against papillary urothelial carcinoma (CIS is flat, so moderate not absolute) [PMC8000909; Pathology Outlines bladder CIS].
- -ct_finding(no_mass_no_wall_thickening_no_nodes): negative cross-sectional imaging argues against established/invasive cancer [PMC8000909; MDPI Cancers 13:1396].
- -smoking_status(lifelong_non_smoker): removes the single greatest bladder-cancer risk factor (~half of cases) [Cleveland Clinic; PMC9411696].
- -mechanism reactive_inflammatory_atypia_against_ca (fires ONCE, lr 0.5): the same atypia read as reactive (not neoplastic) down-weights carcinoma — counted once, not per-finding [PMID 3856982; PMID 11186722].
Note the cytology finding still fires POSITIVE (+1.0986) toward carcinoma at face value, so the answer is not engineered to exclude cancer; the negative discriminators and reactive-atypia mechanism outweigh it.

OPEN UNCERTAINTIES (counterfactual / value-of-information): The TB-vs-malignancy question is formally unresolved pending microbiologic + tissue TB testing. Counterfactual panel: a positive urine TB test or positive tissue granuloma/AFB/PCR pushes GU-TB to ~0.999; tissue carcinoma-confirmed would raise the carcinoma posterior from 0.025 to 0.186 (still below the 30% decision line) and lower GU-TB to 0.951. The engine reports NO KICKBACK — even best/worst-case resolution of the open uncertainties does not flip the 30% decision — so escalation is for confirmation, not because the decision is in doubt. The strong 0.99 posterior reflects convergent INDEPENDENT evidence (IGRA + refractory course + sterile pyuria + renal calcification) plus two correlated-finding mechanisms each counted once; no single finding was allowed to fire multiple times.

per_case.plain_answer_text:
MOST LIKELY DIAGNOSIS: Bladder schistosomiasis (urinary Schistosoma haematobium infection) involving the right posterior bladder wall, with reactive/inflammatory urothelial changes mimicking malignancy. This is the single best fit, though it must be distinguished from its two main competitors (see below).

Key reasoning supporting schistosomiasis:
- A middle-aged man with years of refractory "chronic prostatitis"-type LUTS (frequency, dysuria/burning, terminal dribbling) that only transiently respond to antibiotics, suggesting the antibiotics were never treating the true cause.
- Cystoscopy shows NOT a discrete tumor but a broad zone of mucosal congestion, edema, and diffuse superficial ulceration localized to one bladder wall — the classic appearance of bilharzial cystitis (early active disease produces "sandy patches," tubercles, congestion, and ulceration).
- Histology of inflammatory granulation tissue, fibrovascular polypoid proliferation, and reactive/atypical hyperplastic urothelium is exactly the pattern schistosomiasis produces; chronic S. haematobium is a recognized cause of urothelial atypia, squamous metaplasia, and ultimately squamous cell carcinoma. Reactive atypia readily yields "atypical cells suspicious for malignancy" on cytology (2 of 3 specimens here), a well-known false-positive trap.
- Mildly elevated urine leukocytes, low-grade prostatic inflammation markers, and unremarkable cross-sectional imaging (no mass, no nodes) are consistent — schisto causes mucosal/mural inflammation that cross-sectional CT often does not flag.
- Renal calcified foci can reflect chronic granulomatous/parasitic disease, though they are nonspecific.

Two important differentials that MUST be excluded before committing:
1. Genitourinary tuberculosis — the T-SPOT returned low-positive, the right renal calcifications and chronic granulomatous ulcerative cystitis with relapsing-on-fluoroquinolone course (fluoroquinolones partially treat TB) all fit TB well. This is the leading alternative and arguably co-equal; the relapse-on-quinolone pattern and granulation-tissue histology are very TB-like.
2. Urothelial carcinoma / carcinoma in situ — cannot be dismissed given suspicious cytology on 2 of 3 samples and focal moderate-to-severe atypical hyperplasia. The whole point of the work-up is that the lesion is masquerading as malignancy.

RECOMMENDED NEXT ACTION:
- Send terminal/concentrated urine and the bladder biopsy tissue for ova/parasite examination: look for S. haematobium eggs (terminal-spined) in urine microscopy (ideally a midday/terminal specimen) and in histology; add schistosomal serology. Take a focused exposure/travel history for endemic-area residence or freshwater contact.
- Simultaneously rule out TB: send urine for AFB smear, mycobacterial culture, and TB PCR (NAAT) on urine and on biopsy tissue; have pathology specifically look for caseating granulomas and stain for AFB.
- Have an experienced uropathologist re-examine the biopsy with these two infections explicitly in mind, and obtain deeper/repeat cold-cup biopsies of the abnormal mucosa (and consider biopsy of any sandy patches) to confidently exclude carcinoma in situ before attributing everything to an infection.
- Treat based on the result: praziquantel for confirmed schistosomiasis; full anti-tuberculous therapy if TB is confirmed; do NOT continue empiric fluoroquinolones.

CONFIDENCE: Moderate (~55-60%) for schistosomiasis as the single most likely answer. Confidence is tempered because GU tuberculosis is a strong, almost co-equal contender (the relapsing fluoroquinolone response, renal calcification, positive T-SPOT, and granulomatous ulcerative histology all favor TB), and malignancy is not yet definitively excluded. The decisive step is parasitologic/microbiologic confirmation plus expert pathology, which will quickly separate these three.
per_case.rationale:
Ground truth: the confirmed diagnosis is flat high-grade carcinoma in situ (CIS) of the bladder, mislabeled for ~2 years as chronic prostatitis, confirmed by urine cytology (2/3 atypical) + cystoscopy (diffuse congestion/edema/ulceration, NOT a papillary mass) and definitive TUR pathology; correct disposition is TUR + intravesical BCG. The key teaching point is precisely that flat CIS mimics chronic prostatitis/cystitis, is invisible on CT, and demands cytology + cystoscopy (and ultimately resection/biopsy).

NEITHER output names CIS as the most likely diagnosis, so neither is fully correct. The decisive question is how each handled the malignancy possibility and the confirmatory pathway.

OUTPUT A: Ranks genitourinary TB as the answer at P=0.9924 and actively DRIVES DOWN bladder urothelial carcinoma to P=0.0248, explicitly treating the suspicious 2/3 cytology and moderate-to-severe atypical hyperplasia as "reactive inflammatory atypia." This is the worst possible failure mode for this case: it takes the exact findings that ground truth used to make the CIS diagnosis (positive cytology, severe atypia, flat ulcerative non-mass lesion, negative CT — all CIS-typical) and reinterprets them to nearly exclude cancer. Its "discriminators against carcinoma" (non-smoker, no mass on CT, no discrete tumor on cystoscopy) are reasoning errors here — flat CIS characteristically produces no mass and negative CT, so A used CIS's defining features as evidence against CIS. It even notes carcinoma cannot be flipped by best/worst-case resolution, i.e., it confidently forecloses the correct answer. The recommended next step (urine AFB/TB NAAT, repeat biopsy with AFB) would not establish the true diagnosis and de-prioritizes TURBT (P=0.122, "below threshold") — yet TUR is exactly what confirmed CIS in reality. The 0.99 calibration is severely overconfident and pointed at the wrong diagnosis. False precision (four-decimal posteriors) compounds the miscalibration.

OUTPUT B: Names urinary schistosomiasis as single best fit — also wrong, and arguably exotic/unsupported (no travel/exposure history given, and S. haematobium is the weakest of its three candidates). However, B is materially better on the dimensions that matter: (1) it keeps urothelial carcinoma/CIS explicitly on the table as a differential that "cannot be dismissed" and even states "the whole point of the work-up is that the lesion is masquerading as malignancy," (2) its confidence is appropriately moderate (~55-60%) and it flags TB as nearly co-equal, (3) critically, its recommended next action includes obtaining deeper/repeat biopsies of the abnormal mucosa and expert uropathology review "to confidently exclude carcinoma in situ before attributing everything to an infection" — this confirmatory step aligns with how the real case was actually resolved (resection/biopsy revealing CIS). B's calibration is honest (it does not overclaim), and its disposition would plausibly surface the true diagnosis, whereas A's would not.

Defensibility: A dresses up its reasoning in citations and posteriors but the logic is unsound for flat CIS and the citations don't rescue an answer that excludes the correct diagnosis by design. B's reasoning chain is transparent and self-aware about its own uncertainty.

Winner: B — not because schistosomiasis is right, but because B preserves the correct diagnosis as a live possibility, calibrates confidence appropriately, and recommends the confirmatory biopsy/cytology pathway that actually yields CIS, while A confidently and explicitly drives the correct answer to ~2.5% and would never confirm it.

per_case.ground_truth: Final confirmed diagnosis: Infiltrative hepatic angiosarcoma. The presentation was misleading because the clinical picture (ascites with a high serum-ascites albumin gradient indicating portal hypertension, splenomegaly, cytopenias, cholestatic liver chemistries) strongly mimicked decompensated cirrhosis, yet the patient had no cirrhosis risk factors and an exhaustive workup for infectious (Coxiella, Bartonella, Brucella), viral (hepatitis A/B/D), metabolic/genetic (alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, hemochromatosis), autoimmune, and vascular (Budd-Chiari) causes was negative; ascitic cytology was negative and bone marrow aspirate/flow cytometry were unrevealing. The key discriminator was the diffuse INFILTRATIVE pattern (no discrete liver masses), splenic lesions on CT, and FDG uptake in liver, spleen, and bone marrow on PET-CT. CONFIRMED by liver biopsy: atypical spindle-cell proliferation with hyperchromatic nuclei and scant pale eosinophilic cytoplasm growing along the hepatic sinusoids, with nuclear positivity for the endothelial marker ERG on immunohistochemistry (vascular/endothelial malignancy). Correct disposition: this is an aggressive, near-uniformly fatal malignancy; given advanced age and comorbidities the appropriate course was a goals-of-care discussion. The family elected comfort/palliative care and the patient died a few weeks later. Teaching point: cirrhosis-mimicking portal hypertension with cytopenias, a cholestatic pattern, splenic lesions, marrow FDG avidity, and NO cirrhosis risk factors should prompt a tissue diagnosis to catch infiltrative hepatic malignancy such as angiosarcoma.

TOP CONCLUSION — hepatosplenic infiltrative lymphoma (intravascular large B-cell / hepatosplenic lymphoma). KEY FIRED CLAUSES:

per_case.plain_answer_text:
MOST LIKELY DIAGNOSIS: Hepatosplenic infiltration by a hematolymphoid neoplasm presenting as non-cirrhotic portal hypertension — most specifically a primary hepatosplenic lymphoma, with hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma (HSTCL) or another non-Hodgkin lymphoma (e.g., intravascular large B-cell lymphoma, or splenic marginal-zone lymphoma) at the top of the differential. The single best unifying explanation is diffuse sinusoidal/portal lymphomatous infiltration of liver, spleen, and marrow.

WHY THIS FITS:
- The defining clue is portal hypertension WITHOUT cirrhosis: SAAG >1.1 g/dL (portal-hypertensive) but ascitic total protein 0.9 g/dL. A high-SAAG/low-protein fluid points to a sinusoidal/pre-sinusoidal process. Combined with a thorough negative work-up for cirrhosis (viral, autoimmune, A1AT, hemochromatosis, vascular/Budd-Chiari excluded) and no risk factors, this is "non-cirrhotic portal hypertension" — classically caused by infiltrative disease of the hepatic sinusoids/portal tracts rather than fibrosis.
- A cholestatic-predominant pattern (ALP 540, AST>ALT, bilirubin 3.1) with no discrete dominant mass is the signature of diffuse infiltration of the liver (hepatic sinusoidal/portal infiltration), not focal tumor or biliary obstruction.
- Splenomegaly + multiple splenic lesions + bicytopenia (anemia + thrombocytopenia) + diffuse FDG avidity across liver, spleen, AND bone marrow is the classic hepato-spleno-marrow tropism of lymphoma — particularly HSTCL and intravascular large B-cell lymphoma, both of which characteristically lack a discrete nodal/hepatic mass and instead infiltrate sinusoids/marrow.
- Negative bone marrow aspirate and negative peripheral flow do NOT exclude lymphoma: HSTCL and intravascular lymphoma are notoriously occult on aspirate/flow (patchy, sinusoidal/intravascular distribution) and require tissue architecture (core biopsy with immunohistochemistry) to diagnose. So the "unrevealing" marrow is expected, not reassuring.
- Negative ascitic cytology is also expected — lymphomatous/infiltrative portal hypertension seldom sheds malignant cells into fluid.

KEY ALTERNATIVES TO KEEP ON THE LIST:
- Other infiltrative causes of non-cirrhotic portal hypertension with hepatosplenomegaly: systemic mastocytosis, sarcoidosis (hepatic granulomatous/nodular regenerative hyperplasia), amyloidosis, and a myeloproliferative neoplasm/myelofibrosis with extramedullary hematopoiesis (which can give marrow + hepatosplenic FDG signal and cytopenias). Disseminated infection (e.g., visceral leishmaniasis, miliary TB, fungal — splenic lesions + marrow + cytopenias) is also possible despite the negative zoonotic serologies, though the absence of fever/constitutional infection markers and the chronic "failing" course favor neoplasm.

RECOMMENDED NEXT ACTION (most likely to clinch it): Obtain diagnostic TISSUE from the most accessible involved compartment with full histopathology — a percutaneous/transjugular core LIVER biopsy (transjugular if coagulopathy/ascites/thrombocytopenia preclude percutaneous, and it lets you measure the hepatic venous pressure gradient to confirm sinusoidal portal hypertension) PLUS a bone-marrow CORE (trephine) biopsy — not just aspirate — sent for immunohistochemistry, T- and B-cell clonality (TCR/IGH rearrangement), flow on tissue, and stains for amyloid, mast cells (CD117/tryptate), granulomas, and organisms. Splenic-lesion or PET-directed (most FDG-avid site) biopsy is a reasonable alternative target. Add peripheral smear review, LDH, ferritin, SPEP/free light chains, and infectious tissue cultures/stains in parallel.

CONFIDENCE: Moderate (~55–65%) that the unifying diagnosis is a hepatosplenic lymphoma/hematolymphoid infiltration causing non-cirrhotic portal hypertension; high confidence (~90%) that the correct framing is an INFILTRATIVE cause of non-cirrhotic portal hypertension and that the decisive next step is targeted tissue biopsy (liver core ± transjugular with HVPG, plus marrow trephine and/or PET-directed lesion biopsy). The specific lymphoma subtype is the part with most residual uncertainty.
per_case.rationale:
GROUND TRUTH: The confirmed diagnosis is infiltrative hepatic ANGIOSARCOMA — a vascular/endothelial malignancy (ERG+ spindle cells along hepatic sinusoids), NOT a hematolymphoid neoplasm. Neither output names angiosarcoma. So neither nails the specific entity. The discriminating question for judging is therefore: (a) how well each captures the correct FRAMING (an infiltrative, non-cirrhotic, sinusoidal malignancy requiring tissue diagnosis), (b) how appropriate the recommended confirmatory step is (liver biopsy — the actual confirmatory test), and (c) calibration — is the confidence proportionate to the fact that the leading specific guess (lymphoma) is WRONG.

SHARED CORRECTNESS: Both correctly identify the meta-level framing the ground truth emphasizes — non-cirrhotic portal hypertension from a diffuse INFILTRATIVE process, with the negative cirrhosis workup, splenic lesions, and tri-compartment FDG avidity as the discriminators. Both correctly drive toward tissue biopsy as the decisive next step, which matches the ground truth's confirmatory move (liver biopsy). Both correctly note that negative marrow aspirate/flow and negative cytology do NOT exclude infiltrative malignancy. This framing is the most transferable teaching point, and both get it.

SHARED ERROR: Both anchor on hepatosplenic/intravascular LYMPHOMA as the single best specific diagnosis. This is wrong vs ground truth (angiosarcoma, a vascular sarcoma). Notably, neither output lists angiosarcoma or hepatic vascular malignancy anywhere in its differential, despite the case being a near-textbook presentation (infiltrative pattern, no discrete mass, sinusoidal growth, splenic lesions) — angiosarcoma is a recognized cirrhosis-mimicking infiltrative hepatic malignancy and arguably should have appeared. This is a real miss for both.

CALIBRATION — THE DECISIVE DIFFERENCE: Output A states ~55-65% confidence on the specific lymphoma diagnosis and ~90% only on the FRAMING (infiltrative non-cirrhotic portal HTN + biopsy as next step). Given that the specific diagnosis is actually WRONG but the framing is RIGHT, A's calibration is excellent: it placed high confidence exactly where it was correct (framing/next step) and appropriately hedged where it was wrong (subtype). A explicitly flags subtype as the residual uncertainty. Output B, by contrast, reports a 98.8% posterior on hepatosplenic infiltrative lymphoma — extreme, near-certain confidence on a diagnosis that is WRONG. This is a serious miscalibration: maximal confidence on the incorrect answer. B's elaborate pseudo-quantitative machinery (logits, LRs, VOI, counterfactual panel, citations) projects false precision onto an incorrect conclusion. B does include a self-aware caveat ("framework saturation tension... top posterior reads 98.8% while confirmatory biopsy uncertainty is still open"), which is to its credit, but it does not actually temper the headline number — it surfaces the tension while still presenting 98.8% as the verdict. The confident-but-wrong number is exactly the failure mode calibration scoring penalizes.

DEFENSIBILITY/HALLUCINATION: B's citations (specific PMC IDs, DOIs, logit values to 4 decimals) are largely unverifiable and create an appearance of rigor that the actual (incorrect) conclusion does not earn; several precise numbers (e.g., prior 0.22, LR 6.0, VOI 4.382 logits) are not defensibly derivable from the case and read as fabricated precision. A's reasoning is traceable in plain clinical logic without inventing numbers it cannot support. A's broader differential (mastocytosis, sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, MPN/myelofibrosis, disseminated infection) is also more appropriately wide for an undiagnosed infiltrative syndrome, leaving more room for the true answer even though it too omits angiosarcoma.

VERDICT: Both miss the specific diagnosis identically (lymphoma instead of angiosarcoma), both get the framing and next step right. A wins clearly on calibration — it is appropriately uncertain about the specific call it got wrong and confident only about the framing it got right — whereas B asserts 98.8% certainty on the wrong diagnosis and dresses it in unverifiable precision. Calibration and defensibility are the tiebreakers, and they favor A decisively.

per_case.ground_truth:
FINAL CONFIRMED DIAGNOSIS: Hairy cell leukemia (HCL), a rare chronic B-cell lymphoproliferative malignancy. It was masquerading as hepatitis B virus (HBV)-related cirrhosis with hypersplenism in a chronically HBV-infected patient who presented with massive splenomegaly and pancytopenia.

HOW CONFIRMED: Definitive diagnosis was made by SPLENIC HISTOPATHOLOGY after splenectomy, showing the pathognomonic features of HCL with immunohistochemistry positive for the B-cell marker CD20 (HCL classically co-expresses CD20/CD19/CD22 with CD11c, CD25, CD103, and Annexin A1; BRAF V600E is the driver mutation). The initial bone marrow examination was misleading/non-diagnostic (HCL marrow is fibrotic and characteristically yields a 'dry tap', which can mimic or be mistaken for other processes).

KEY DISCRIMINATORS that pointed away from cirrhosis: despite massive splenomegaly, the patient's LIVER FUNCTION TESTS WERE NORMAL with INTACT COAGULATION/synthetic function — inconsistent with decompensated cirrhotic portal hypertension; and the SPLEEN WAS DISPROPORTIONATELY LARGE relative to what cirrhotic portal hypertension typically produces. The combination of HBV positivity, splenomegaly, and pancytopenia had anchored clinicians on HBV cirrhosis + hypersplenism.

CORRECT DISPOSITION/TREATMENT: First-line therapy for HCL is a purine analogue (cladribine or pentostatin), often with rituximab (anti-CD20); BRAF inhibitors (vemurafenib) are options for relapsed/refractory disease. In THIS case, splenectomy was performed (diagnostic + palliative, relieving compressive symptoms and hypersplenism); the patient declined systemic chemotherapy for financial reasons and survived >20 months. Published in Hepatitis Monthly 2026;26(1):e168731 (Wu X, Huang Z, Gan Q, Wang B).
